phonemes.desc: Short mid-front [e] gliding toward [a]; the two vowels of 'each' run close together in Gaelic speech.
Voiceless velar fricative [x], the rasp of Scottish 'loch' — never the hard k the English eye expects.
Close back unrounded [ɯ] shading to [ɯʃ]; the Gaelic ui has no clean English equivalent — think of a compressed 'oo-ish'.
Palatalized [ɡʲ], a slender g with a y-glide, closing on the short unstressed schwa [ə].

pronunciation.approximation: EKH-ooshkya — stress the first syllable, let the ch rasp as in 'loch', and run the second word tight: the whole compound is one breath, horse and water together.

kin.label: Old Irish

kin.label: Manx
kin.form: cabbyl-ushtey, the Isle of Man's water-horse — same sense, related words

kin.label: Lowland Scots
kin.form: kelpie — the river-haunting cousin; a different word, not a cognate, for a kindred power

pronunciation.note: Eachuisge is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Gaelic compound is written in plain Latin letters — no diacritic and no distinctive character for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone marks the temple form; the creature's standing in the folklore record is beside the point. The hyphens of the dictionaries (each-uisge) are a grammatical courtesy, not a registrable form.

domains.title: The Water Horse of the Lochs
domains.subtitle: The Perfect Stallion, the Adhesive Back, and the Liver That Floated Ashore
domains.lead: Eachuisge — the each-uisge, the water horse — is the most dangerous being in the Highland Otherworld: a shape-shifter that haunts the lochs and sea-lochs of Gaelic Scotland, wearing the shape of a flawless stallion at the water's edge. Mount him and your hands stick fast to his hide; the loch does the rest. The Lowland kelpie haunts rivers and is content to drown you — the each-uisge devours.

cards.name: The Loch
cards.desc: His true country: the deep freshwater lochs and sea-lochs of the Highlands, where he waits beneath the surface.

cards.name: The Perfect Stallion
cards.desc: His chosen lure: a beautiful horse standing tame by the shore, offered to any traveler in a hurry.

cards.name: The Adhesive Back
cards.desc: Once mounted, the rider cannot dismount: the hide holds the hand like pitch, and the horse runs for the water.

cards.name: The Handsome Stranger
cards.desc: His other shape: a fine young man by the shore — betrayed, the tales say, by the water-weed in his hair.

symbols.name: The flawless stallion
symbols.meaning: The too-perfect gift at the water's edge — beauty as bait, offered where the ground runs out

symbols.name: The adhesive hide
symbols.meaning: The choice that cannot be unmade: once mounted, the mount decides

symbols.name: The liver on the shore
symbols.meaning: The one thing the loch gives back — the Highland record's grimmest detail, and its proof that this horse devours

symbols.name: The weed in the stranger's hair
symbols.meaning: The tell the shape cannot shed: water keeps its mark on whatever walks out of it

mythology.lead: The each-uisge has no medieval manuscript behind him: his mythology is oral, and its primary witnesses are the great nineteenth-century field collections of the Highlands — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. The tales agree on the essentials with the consistency of a warning passed from shore to shore.

myths.title: The Rider Taken
myths.text: The core of every telling is the same. A traveler on the shore of a loch finds a beautiful horse standing idle — fine beyond any horse in the parish, saddled by luck, or so it seems. He mounts; the horse is smooth and willing; and then the rider finds his hands fast to the hide, stuck as if with bird-lime, and the horse's head already turned toward the water. The loch takes them both. In the grimmest tellings the loch gives the rider back in pieces — the tradition is exact about this: the each-uisge devours the whole body, and what floats ashore is the liver alone. That detail is the Highland folklore's way of drawing the line between its own water horse and the Lowland kelpie, which drowns but does not eat.

myths.title: The Boy Who Cut Off His Finger
myths.text: The best-known of the warning-tales gives the creature a longer game. A fine horse appears to children playing by a loch, and one by one they climb its back — and the back lengthens to take them, seat after seat, until all are mounted save one wary boy, who will only touch the hide with a finger. The horse springs for the water with its load of children, and the boy, stuck by that single finger, does the one thing left: he cuts the finger off and escapes. The loch gives back the others the next day, piecemeal. The collectors recorded the tale across the Highlands, and Briggs notes it among the each-uisge's defining episodes: the compound's lesson compressed into a single image — touch with everything and you lose everything; touch with a finger and a finger pays for the lesson.

myths.title: The Handsome Stranger
myths.text: The horse is only the working shape. The each-uisge also walks ashore as a fine young man, and the tales of the loch-side courting are as consistent as the tales of the ride. A girl meets a handsome stranger by the water; he lays his head in her lap and sleeps; and as she combs his hair with her fingers she finds in it the sand and weed of the loch bottom. She understands what is sleeping on her knee, eases her skirt free, and runs — and behind her the shape comes apart into horse and water. The weed in the hair is the tradition's signature: the shape-shifter can borrow any face but cannot shed the mark of the element he came from.

myths.title: The Red-Hot Iron
myths.text: The record also remembers that the each-uisge can be killed, and how. Ordinary iron and ordinary courage fail against a thing that lives in the water; the answer the tales keep is fire carried into iron. In the well-known Highland account preserved by John Gregorson Campbell, a smith destroys a water horse with a red-hot iron — a spear or bar heated in the forge and driven home while the creature is held fast. The pattern is the old one the collectors noted across Gaelic tradition: the supernatural yields to the smith, whose craft joins the two elements the water horse cannot master — fire, and the metal that remembers it. The tale matters to the record because it is nearly unique: almost everything else the Highlands says about the each-uisge is a way to avoid him.

lore.syncretism: The each-uisge is the Highland head of a family that runs the length of the Celtic coasts and beyond. His closest cousin is the Lowland Scots kelpie, which haunts rivers rather than lochs and is generally the milder power — drowning without devouring; the two are kindred, not cognate, for the words are unrelated. The Northern Isles keep their own: Shetland's nuggle or njogel, and Orkney's nuckelavee, a far worse thing — a skinless fusion of man and horse that must be distinguished from the shape-shifting water horse proper. The Isle of Man has the cabbyl-ushtey, Wales the ceffyl dŵr, and Ireland the each-uisce and the shape-shifting [[pooka|Púca]], which takes horse-shape among its many forms. The tradition is older than the collections: [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]]'s horse Aonbharr, which runs over land and sea alike, shows the medieval Irish imagination already at work on the horse that owns both elements. Beyond the Celtic world the type recurs — the Scandinavian bäckahäst and the nøkk among them — and the handbooks treat the whole complex as one of the most widespread figure-types of northern European water-lore: the horse as the beautiful face of drowning.
lore.culturalLegacy: The each-uisge entered print through the great Victorian field collections — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–62) and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900) — and it never left. Katharine Briggs's Encyclopedia of Fairies fixed its modern profile as the fiercest of the British water-horses, and MacKillop's Dictionary of Celtic Mythology carried it into the standard Celtic reference shelf. Burns had already put the Lowland cousin into verse — the 'water-kelpie' of the Address to the Deil — and the whole water-horse tradition stands behind the Highlands' most famous modern legend: commentators have long read the loch-monster lore of the twentieth century against this older record of horses in the water. Andy Scott's Kelpies at Falkirk (2013), the thirty-meter horse-head sculptures on the Forth and Clyde Canal, are the tradition's monumental afterlife — kelpies by name, but the image they make permanent is the each-uisge's own: the horse rising out of Scottish water. In Gaelic itself the compound never went anywhere: each-uisge still means the water horse, and the warning it carries is older than any collection that preserves it.
lore.extendedMeditation:
The each-uisge is the most honest monster in the Celtic record, because its method is consent. It does not chase, does not strike, does not break down any door. It stands at the water's edge in the shape of the one thing a tired traveler most wants — a beautiful horse, unclaimed, waiting — and it lets the victim do the approaching. Everything that follows follows from a single step: the moment of mounting. After that there is no further decision to make, and that is the horror the Highland tellers kept sharpening — the adhesive hide, the back that lengthens to take one more, the hands that will not come free.

The tradition is not superstition in the cheap sense; it is risk assessment in story form. Water in the Highlands is deep, cold, and patient, and the loch that will drown you looks exactly like the loch that will carry your boat. The each-uisge personifies that double face: the surface that offers itself and the depth that keeps what it takes. And its one consistent weakness is the oldest rule of the shore — touch with a finger first, and be ready to lose the finger rather than the rest.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is the ordinary Gaelic common-noun compound each-uisge, 'water horse', written in the Latin alphabet Gaelic has used since the early medieval period — normalized here as Eachuisge for the temple form. There is no older monumental attestation: the figure belongs to oral tradition, and its primary record is the nineteenth-century field collection, not the manuscript codex. The compound is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the restoration changes nothing but the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: eachuisge.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: The each-uisge has no material witness, and the record must be exact about what that means: no inscription names him, no manuscript illuminates him, and no medieval codex preserves his tales, because he belongs to oral tradition rather than to the literary cycles. His primary evidence is the nineteenth-century field collection — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–62), gathered from Gaelic-speaking informants across the western Highlands and Islands, and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900), the fullest single dossier of the water horse's habits. Carmichael's Carmina Gadelica records the same Highland world in its charms and invocations. The landscape itself is the rest of the evidence: the deep freshwater lochs and sea-lochs of the west are the named settings of the tales, and the water-horse complex they belong to is one of the most widely attested figure-types in northern European folklore — a fact the comparatists established from the collections, not from the ground.
